t: How To Make Time-Out A Stronger Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/08/28/how-to-make-time-out-a-stronger-consequence/
q: In other words, time-out needs to be about as much fun as dropping a dumbbell on your toes.
Your students must know exactly how to go to time-out, what they’re required to do once they’re there, and what they must do to rejoin their classmates.
Don’t add to it by lecturing, scolding, or showing displeasure. These methods weaken time-out by lifting the weight of accountability off of your students’ shoulders.
Most teachers remove students from time-out too soon. For most students, five or ten minutes won’t have the desired effect.
When a student says they’re ready to leave time-out, let them do the talking. If you’re satisfied with their level of contrition, smile and invite them back.
After completing time-out, allow the student to return to being a regular member of your classroom—in good standing. Don’t hold a grudge.
For time-out to be a strong consequence, it must be an emotional, as well as physical, separation.

t: A Forbidden Classroom Management Strategy You Should Be Using https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/08/21/a-forbidden-classroom-management-strategy/
q: The forbidden strategy I’m referring to has gotten a bad rap, but is so effective it’s used to train nurses, police officers, professional athletes, and opera singers.
In the hands of an unskilled or impatient teacher, students can become bored, resentful, and likely to cause trouble.
Repetition should come only after baseline learning takes place. Teach and model routines thoroughly before asking students to practice them.
Practice each routine only twice in a row. Then take a break from that particular routine. Your students will learn faster if you come back and practice later in the day—or the next one.
Only repeat a routine done incorrectly. If your students get it right, tell them they were perfect and move on to something else.
Routines are about pride—pride in doing something well, pride in being part of a special group, and pride in standing apart from the crowd.

t: A Simple, Effective Homework Plan For Teachers: Part 2
q: Collecting homework is a waste of time. Here’s why: Upon return, nearly all students will stuff it in their desk or backpack and not give it another thought.
Instead of collecting it, have your students pair up and cross check their answers. Why? Because it adds ownership, motivation, and accountability to homework.
It’s done. You squeezed all the learning you needed from it. Now it’s time to throw the homework away. There is no reason to keep it.
Ask your students to crumble up their homework, and on your signal, shoot it at the basket.
Any student who comes to school without homework completed, and doesn’t get it finished during partner check, must do it at home that evening along with the homework assigned for the day.
